newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl dismisses talk of German cabinet reshuffle.
newsitem.headline: Kohl dismisses talk of German cabinet reshuffle.

text.p: German Chancellor Helmut Kohl on Monday dismissed speculation that he planned to reshuffle his cabinet next year before a general election in 1998.
"I'm satisfied with my ministers," Kohl remarked when asked about comments by Finance Minister Theo Waigel about possible changes in the cabinet.
Waigel touched off the speculation with an interview in this week's Focus magazine in which he said: "Kohl has to line up in 1997 the team he wants to govern with in the year 2000."
Waigel said the planned closing of the postal ministry after privatisation in 1997 meant a shift of the balance of power within the centre-right government.

His Christian Social Union party, Bavarian sister party to Kohl's Christian Democrats (CDU), would need another high-level post to compensate for the loss of the postal portfolio it now holds, he indicated in the interview.

The CSU has 50 deputies in the 672-seat parliament, three more than the liberal Free Democrats who round out Kohl's coalition. Losing the postal ministry would mean it had only three cabinet seats, the same total as the FDP.

Also on Monday, Waigel and CDU general secretary Peter Hintze both warned the FDP against flirting with the opposition Social Democrats in a bid to engineer a shift of power in Bonn after the 1998 vote.

According to German press reports, Kohl's former FDP vice-chancellor Juergen Moellemann has been trying to arrange an SPD-FDP coalition in Germany's most populous state, North Rhine- Westphalia, in preparation for a power shift in Bonn.
The current state coalition of SPD and Greens has bogged down in local squabbles and SPD leaders there are reported to be eager to ditch the environmentalists.

Der Spiegel magazine said Kohl told newspaper editors at a confidential briefing last week that he was watching events there carefully and thought his own coalition could not continue in 1998 if the state government shifted to SPD-FDP.

SPD-FDP coalitions governed in Bonn from 1969 to 1982 under Chancellors Willy Brandt and Helmut Schmidt. This shift to the left on the national level was preceded by an SPD-FDP coalition in North Rhine-Westphalia.

Spiegel quoted Kohl as saying his party, which now stands at 40 percent in public opinion polls, would have to aim for the nearly impossible goal of an absolute majority in 1998 if it could not depend on the FDP to return it to power.

"The audience was listening so intently that none of the journalists asked if Kohl would run again in such an emergency," Spiegel wrote. "The chancellor thanked them for this oversight and said 'I wouldn't have answered'."
